newsitem.title: USA: BOXING-HOLYFIELD LEANS TOWARD TYSON REMATCH BUT NOT IN MARCH.
newsitem.headline: BOXING-HOLYFIELD LEANS TOWARD TYSON REMATCH BUT NOT IN MARCH.

text.p: Evander Holyfield dictated his fight with Mike Tyson last week and on Saturday he reminded him the new champion is still in charge.
Holyfield, using the new king of the hill's prerogative, said he would not let Tyson push him into a rematch in March, despite Tyson's insistent prodding on Saturday.

Holyfield, in New York on a satellite hookup with Tyson in Ohio, would not commit to fighting Tyson again. But it was clear he is leaning toward a rematch that could earn him even more than the $30 million Tyson received as the champion for last Saturday's fight. Holyfield received $11 million.

The three-time heavyweight champion said, "I look forward (to a rematch). I just don't want to go into it too fast. I do have shoulder problems. I think March is too soon. I won't be able to be prepared for it."

Tyson was speaking from his Southington, Ohio, home where for part of the interview he was lounging -- dressed in a black shirt and black leather pants with matching suspenders -- on a huge bed with a zebra-stripped bedspread and his new tiger cub chewing on his elbow.

From what "Evander is saying over there in New York, he's not speaking like someone with any zest for a rematch," Tyson said, adding when there was great interest in a rematch with any of his previous opponents he was quick to say, 'let's fight again.'"

But a resplendent Holyfield, adhering to the animal-themed fashion of the day in a black shirt and black pants with a shimmering, bright yellow, leopard-patterened vest, would not be pushed into announcing a rematch.

"I know my body and it caused me to lose the championship to Riddick Bowe," said Holyfield referring to his 1992 bout with Bowe, the first of their three fights. "I'm not going in there unprepared and find myself at a disadvantage. I have great respect for Mike Tyson."

Throughout the interview for a programme surrounding the rebroadcast of their fight on Showtime cable television on Sunday, Tyson insisted he did not remember much of the beating he had taken in Las Vegas in losing his World Boxing Association heavyweight title to Holyfield.

In fact, when he returned to his dressing room after Holyfield stopped him in the 11th round with a devastating barrage of punches, "the first thing I said was, 'what happened.' I had thought I knocked Holyfield out. I didn't know I had lost."

Holyfield and Tyson were very respectful of each other on Saturday, with Tyson saying Holyfield fought a "great fight." But Tyson said, without elaborating, "I discovered some very interesting things about Mr. Holyfield. I look forward to the rematch in March."
The host of the interview said Tyson could not be in New York because of the terms of his parole, referring to his release in March, 1995, after serving three years in prison on a rape conviction.
Tyson shot back: "Don't tell my damn business, okay?"
That section was done over and the host just said in the version to be rebroadcast, "circumstances" had kept Tyson in Ohio.
Asked whether he would retain his cornermen, who were criticised for not guiding Tyson to adjust to Holyfield's attack, Tyson said they "absolutely" would return.
"If they told me anything, trust me, it was appropriate advice. I just wasn't coherent to take it."
Tyson said when he returned to his corner after the first round he was asked how he felt, and said, "'I'm in good shape. I can fight like this all night.'"
Tyson was asked what he was thinking at one point in the fight and said, as the tape rolled: "Oh, Man, I don't know what I'm doing here. This is really bizarre."
Tyson insisted Holyfield did not knocke him down with a particularly strong punch in the sixth round.
"That wasn't a legitimate knockdown," said Tyson. "I was a little bit off balance."
But then he added, referring to his confusion in the fight: "I probably thought I knocked him down."
